strengths: Well-motivated technical contribution: casts Deletion/Insertion metric optimization as a permutation-learning problem and uses Gumbel-Sinkhorn to obtain a differentiable relaxation of sorting/top-k selection, enabling direct end-to-end optimization of the actual evaluation metrics rather than surrogate/heuristic objectives used by prior amortized explainers.

Thoughtfully engineered training pipeline (region-based permutation, perturbation-step sampling, grid augmentation, spurious-peak regularization) that makes the otherwise expensive full-sequence AUC optimization tractable at high resolution, with clear ablations (Fig. 3) justifying these choices.

Retains single-forward-pass amortized inference efficiency while offering an optional few-step test-time refinement that provides a clean compute/quality trade-off, and is shown to be useful even for detecting an injected shortcut feature in an out-of-distribution fine-tuned model (Sec. A.3), which is a nice, non-trivial demonstration of the method's flexibility.

Broad empirical validation: two ViT backbones and a CNN (ConvNeXt) backbone, multiple faithfulness metrics (Deletion/Insertion, Positive/Negative, ADP/PIC), multiple reference-image protocols, an apples-to-apples comparison under the MDA evaluation protocol, full-curve AUC plots, and extensive qualitative comparisons in the appendix.

Consistent quantitative gains together with markedly lower runtime than the strongest perturbation- and metric-optimization baselines (e.g., 3+ orders of magnitude faster than MDA while matching or beating it), and qualitatively sharper, boundary-aligned pixel-level maps compared to patch-level ViT attribution baselines.
Honest discussion of limitations (need to retrain per target model, proxy nature of Deletion/Insertion, dependence on representative training data).
weaknesses: The explainer relies on a large frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 encoder, which is substantially larger than the target models being explained (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt-S). This raises questions about how much of the attribution quality stems from strong pretrained visual features versus the proposed learning-to-rank objective itself, and about the fairness of runtime/efficiency comparisons if backbone training/inference cost is considered.

No direct comparison against other learning-based/amortized attribution baselines (e.g., FastSHAP, L2X-style self-supervised amortizers, or other proxy-objective explainers mentioned in Related Work); all learned-model comparisons are against a single per-sample optimization baseline (MDA), leaving the claimed advantage over the broader amortized-explainer category only qualitatively argued rather than empirically demonstrated.

Because the model is trained to directly optimize (differentiable surrogates of) the same Deletion/Insertion metrics used for evaluation, there is a risk of metric-specific overfitting/gaming; while Positive/Negative and ADP/PIC partially mitigate this concern, these are conceptually related perturbation-based metrics, and no metric that is truly independent of the perturbation paradigm (e.g., human evaluation or a localization/segmentation-based ground truth) is used to validate the qualitative 'boundary-alignment' claims.

The per-target-model retraining requirement is a meaningful practical limitation for many use cases (e.g., quickly explaining a newly trained or fine-tuned model), and while test-time refinement is proposed as a partial remedy, its effectiveness for models substantially different from the training-time target is only demonstrated in a narrow, constructed shortcut-detection scenario rather than systematically.

Region-based training with mean-pooled, grid-based permutation could bias the learned ranking toward regional rather than fine-grained pixel importance, and the effect of the L2 smoothness regularizer on suppressing genuinely important small/localized features is not analyzed.

The paper provides limited discussion of hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., temperature, Sinkhorn iterations, loss weighting) and no error bars/statistical significance testing across the large tables of results.

strengths: The core idea—casting Deletion/Insertion-metric optimization as a differentiable permutation-learning problem via Gumbel-Sinkhorn relaxation—is a reasonably novel and technically well-motivated way to bypass the non-differentiability of top-k/sorting operations that plague direct metric optimization for attribution.

The paper is thorough in its empirical coverage: three classifier backbones (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ConvNeXt-S), multiple reference-image conditions, and a wide battery of faithfulness metrics (Deletion, Insertion, Positive/Negative, ADP, PIC), with full per-condition tables in the appendix.

Substantial efficiency advantage is convincingly demonstrated: AHA at T=0 is orders of magnitude faster than perturbation-based competitors (e.g., MDA at 13.6s vs. AHA at 0.016s) while remaining competitive or better on most metrics.

The optional test-time refinement mechanism is a sensible design that lets the method trade off compute for quality, and the out-of-distribution shortcut-detection experiment (Sec. A.3) is a nice, concrete illustration of this mechanism's practical value.

Practical training strategies (region-based permutation, perturbation-step subsampling, grid augmentation, smoothness regularization) are clearly motivated and ablated (Fig. 3), showing the authors thought carefully about making the approach tractable at high resolution.
weaknesses: Fundamental circularity concern: the explainer is trained to directly optimize (soft approximations of) the exact Deletion/Insertion metrics used for evaluation. This makes comparisons against methods that were not designed to directly chase this objective somewhat unfair, and more importantly raises the concern that the model may be learning to exploit specific artifacts of the perturbation/masking procedure (e.g., how blank/blurred pixels interact with the classifier) rather than producing genuinely faithful explanations. The paper's limitations section briefly acknowledges metric sensitivity but does not empirically probe this risk (e.g., via model-randomization/sanity checks à la Adebayo et al., which are cited as motivation but never actually run on the proposed method).

No comparison against the closely related amortized/self-supervised explainer baselines explicitly discussed in Related Work (e.g., FastSHAP, L2X/REAL-X-style methods). The paper claims superiority over this literature but never empirically validates it, which weakens the central 'learning-based methods' contribution claim.

The claimed 'dense, pixel-level' attribution is somewhat overstated: the training signal itself is computed at region level via grid pooling (G up to 28, i.e., regions of 8–32px), not at the pixel level. The apparent pixel-level sharpness in qualitative results may be attributable largely to the powerful frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbone and DPT decoder rather than to the proposed metric-optimization objective itself. No ablation isolates the backbone's contribution (e.g., comparing DINOv3 features alone, or a weaker encoder, or a simple heuristic-distillation baseline using the same architecture) to disentangle architecture effects from the proposed training scheme.

Qualitative claims of 'boundary-aligned' and more interpretable explanations rest on a small number of cherry-picked examples (Fig. 1, 4) without any human evaluation/user study to substantiate that the sharper maps are actually more interpretable or trustworthy to end users, as opposed to merely visually different.

Training cost/amortization overhead is not quantified (wall-clock time, GPU-hours to train the explainer per target model), making it hard to assess the true cost-benefit tradeoff against per-sample perturbation methods, especially since a new explainer must be trained for every target model per the stated limitations.

Results are reported without variance/error bars or multiple seeds, and the method is only validated on ImageNet classification; no evidence of generalization to other tasks, datasets, or domains (e.g., dense prediction, medical imaging) despite motivating the work with safety-critical domains like healthcare and autonomous driving.

strengths: Well-motivated formulation that reframes the classic Deletion/Insertion attribution metrics as a permutation-learning problem, enabling end-to-end differentiable optimization via a Gumbel-Sinkhorn relaxation; this cleanly bridges the causal grounding of perturbation-based methods with the efficiency of amortized/learning-based explainers.

The approach directly addresses a well-articulated gap in the literature (propagation vs. perturbation vs. learning-based tradeoffs) and produces dense, pixel-level attributions for ViTs rather than the coarse patch-level maps typical of prior ViT-specific methods, which is a clear practical advantage illustrated convincingly in Fig. 1.

Strong, broad empirical evaluation: two ViT variants and a ConvNeXt classifier, multiple faithfulness metrics (Deletion, Insertion, Positive/Negative, ADP/PIC), three different reference-image protocols, and a dedicated comparison under the MDA evaluation protocol for fairness.

Runtime efficiency is compelling: AHA (T=0) matches the speed of fast propagation-based baselines while being orders of magnitude faster than per-sample optimization methods like MDA, and optional T-step refinement provides a flexible quality/speed tradeoff supported by clear ablations (Fig. 3).
Thoughtful engineering to make training tractable and robust (region-based permutation, perturbation-step subsampling, grid augmentation, peak regularization) is well justified and ablated.
The out-of-distribution shortcut-detection experiment (Appendix A.3) is a nice, creative demonstration of the practical value of the test-time refinement mechanism beyond the main benchmark numbers.
Extensive supplementary material (per-reference-image tables, AUC curves, additional qualitative figures) supports reproducibility and gives a fairly complete picture of method behavior.
weaknesses: The claim of "consistent quantitative improvements" is somewhat optimistic: TIS frequently achieves the best Insertion and PIC scores (e.g., Table 1, Insertion 0.6381 for TIS vs. 0.6112 for AHA at T=0), so AHA's advantage is concentrated in Deletion/Positive-type metrics rather than uniformly across all faithfulness measures at T=0.

The core technical machinery (Gumbel-Sinkhorn differentiable sorting/OT) is adopted from prior work (Mena et al. 2018) rather than newly developed; the paper's novelty lies primarily in its application/framing to attribution rather than in the underlying differentiable-sorting technique itself.

Evaluation is limited to ImageNet classification with a small set of backbones; no experiments on other tasks (e.g., detection/segmentation), other domains (e.g., medical imaging mentioned as a motivating application), or larger/more diverse model families, which somewhat limits evidence for the claimed general applicability.

Practical limitations are non-trivial: retraining is required per target model and access to representative training data is needed, which the paper acknowledges but which meaningfully constrains applicability to proprietary or data-scarce settings (partially mitigated but not fully resolved by refinement).

Offline training cost/time is not reported, making it hard to assess the true amortization trade-off relative to baselines, especially per-sample optimization methods like MDA which incur no training cost.
Quantitative comparison to some directly relevant related work mentioned in the text (e.g., EVA, Less is More) is discussed only qualitatively and not included in the benchmark tables.
